item.title: Owning Harm Without Shame: A Guide for Estranged Parents
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Owning Harm Without Shame: A Guide for Estranged Parents

4 steps for parents to reconnect with distant adult children.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Check your motivation to reconnect with your adult child who has withdrawn from you.
  • Addressing shame is key. Shame can be a barrier to hearing the impact your actions have had.
  • Asking, "Is there more?" demonstrates authentic interest in knowing how they have suffered.
  • Maturing the working definition of love may help parents break cycles of harm.

Headlines regarding estrangement between adult children and parents have become increasingly common. Articles like the Wall Street Journal’s “Why Are So Many Adults Cutting Off Their Parents?” or The Guardian’s “A ‘Silent Epidemic’ of Family Estrangement Is on the Rise” continue to highlight the disconnection of adult children from their parents. This zeitgeist of family division continues despite more experts weighing in. Some have an obvious agenda while others are more subtle.

Rather than dissecting articles or debating statistics, I would like to offer practical steps for parents seeking to reconnect with their adult children. These recommendations are based on my professional experience working both with adult children who have reduced contact for their own well-being, and with parents who feel confused, angry, and hurt by the distance. If your agenda is authentic relationship repair and not just moving through a checklist, these steps are for you.

Source: Martin Porter / Unsplash

Check Your Motivation Level

First, ask yourself, “How much would I like to reconnect with my adult child?” Your answer will predict how much emotional work you are willing to do to work toward repair. Engaging in conversations that address neglect, abuse, and other injury can be very challenging. The following four steps can help.

4 Steps to Reconnect With Your Adult Child

1. Let go of the detailed facts.

If your child remembers a situation differently, look past the specific details and try to understand how the experience affected them. Refocus on the emotional impact rather than debating specific events. No arguing needed; just listen.

2. Manage shame.

Defensiveness and denial often stem from unaddressed shame, which can prevent genuine accountability. Take responsibility for your role in any harm experienced—whether through direct actions or inaction, failing to protect them, or making excuses for others who harmed them.

If your child feels that conversations “always become about you,” shame may be blocking your ability to repair the relationship. Overcoming this requires sitting with that discomfort rather than shielding yourself from it. Shame can flood your nervous system and become a shield that prevents you from apologizing.

Mistakes are normal. Refusing to face them is learned. You may never have intended to cause harm, and you may feel terrible that you did. Gather all the humility you can muster and turn toward whatever is uncomfortable. No blame or groveling needed; just humility and accountability.

3. Pause and ask: “Is there more?”

Avoid rushing the process by asking if things are “all good now.” Instead, acknowledge their pain and say: “I am so sorry. I am just coming to understand the reality of the impact of my actions. Is there more?”

Express a sincere willingness to listen and take responsibility for past actions or inactions. If you notice resistance in yourself to this, dig deeper and inquire within: Why not? Am I doing this for my child’s well-being, or to protect my own image? Ground yourself and watch for the barbs of perfectionism that can lead to more dismissiveness of their concerns. Take them one at a time; no floodgates needed.

4. Re-examine your definition of love.

If your view of family love relies on obligation, denial of harm, or enforcing a long-held family narrative of how things need to be, consider updating that perspective. Upgrade your old understanding of love as defined by your parents, church, community, or culture.

Reconnecting with your adult child requires adopting a definition of love centered on honesty, accountability, and mutual respect. This includes regarding your child as a separate individual—not an extension of yourself. Applaud their efforts to individuate, challenge the norms, and grow.

If the above steps feel overwhelming, seek professional support to help you navigate relationship repair. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: "Your Labs Are Fine" May Be More Dangerous Than You Think
item.description:
Eating Disorders

"Your Labs Are Fine" May Be More Dangerous Than You Think

Labs can be misleading in eating disorder care.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Labs are often normal when someone has an eating disorder.
  • Normal labs do not indicate that someone is not sick from their eating disorder.
  • Reassuring someone that their labs are normal and everything is fine can inadvertently cause harm.

“Your labs look fine” can be some of the most harmful words in eating disorder care.

People often find it surprising when I say that labs are often normal, even when someone is very sick with their eating disorder. That being said, bloodwork gets a lot of attention, and it’s easy to see why. It gives doctors something concrete to do, and they are objective. However, in eating disorder treatment, they are often misleading.

Over the years, patients and families have told me again and again that when they went to their doctor with concerns about an eating disorder, they were reassured. They were told, “Your labs look fine, and there is nothing to worry about.” While this sounds harmless, it isn’t. This reassurance frequently results in a delay of care and potentially worsens the disease, especially given that early intervention is linked to a better prognosis.

There are two specific reasons why we should check labs in someone with an eating disorder who has lost weight.

First, we want to make sure we aren’t missing another cause for weight loss. Children and adolescents shouldn’t be losing weight. When they are losing weight, we need to be sure there aren’t other reasons why. Eating disorders are a diagnosis of exclusion, and we must rule out conditions like diabetes, thyroid disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and celiac disease.

The second reason to check labs is to evaluate for the medical complications of an eating disorder. Weight loss can impact electrolytes, blood counts, vitamin D levels, iron levels, hormone levels, and more.

However, labs do not necessarily tell us how sick someone is. The reality is that labs are often normal when someone is very sick. The wise body does everything it can to protect vital functioning and finds a way to compensate for malnutrition. Therefore, the bloodwork often looks reassuring. Someone can be medically hospitalized with a critically low heart rate and still have normal labs.

Unfortunately, there is real potential harm in saying, “Good news, the labs look good.” For a worried parent who has been witnessing disordered eating behavior, it can give them the message that their concern was unwarranted. And, for the child suffering from the eating disorder, who is feeling ambivalent about getting treatment and working toward recovery or continuing the eating disorder, it can send a message to them that they are not sick enough, and they should keep going.

So, how should we approach the labs? Labs are a small part of the clinical picture. We need to treat them as part of the story and history, along with the trajectory on the growth chart, the resting heart rate and orthostatic vital sign changes, the symptoms, and the history from the patient and their family. And we should follow along over time, since normal labs one day doesn’t mean they will stay normal in the setting of an eating disorder.

For the clinician, if a patient or parent is concerned about eating behaviors and labs are normal, consider saying, “Labs are typically normal in people who have eating disorders, even when someone is very sick. Normal results are good to see, but they don’t tell us that your health isn’t being affected.”

For the parent, if the clinician reassures you that the labs are normal but you are still concerned about your child’s eating behaviors or health, you can ask to speak to an eating disorder specialist and have your child re-evaluated. You heard it from this doctor: Don’t stop at the normal labs, and listen to your gut.

item.title: The Fight for Life on Earth Is Regaining Momentum
item.description:
Environment

The Fight for Life on Earth Is Regaining Momentum

Reflections from the 2026 NYC Climate Week

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Talking about climate change can expand political possibilities and reveal shared concern.
  • Believing that collective action can work is a powerful driver of climate engagement.
  • Climate progress increasingly depends on the information and AI systems shaping public life.
  • Connections across people, institutions, sectors, and countries can build movement momentum.

NYC was buzzing with life, as always, but during Climate Week, something even more exciting was in the air. Everyone was talking about climate change.

My week started with a panel organized by the Environmental Voter Project and the Climate Museum. Nathaniel Stinnett, founder of the EVP, Arnab Pal, CEO of Deploy Action, and I, joined Climate Museum Director Miranda Massie and more than 100 climate leaders across technology, science, health, investment, education, the arts, and politics. I was excited to see my heroine, Dana Fisher, and my fierce graduate student Danielle Goldwert in the audience.

That conversation, and many that followed, left me reenergized. Despite frantic opposition from the fossil fuel sector, I saw many of the psychological conditions that allow social movements to build momentum. People are talking, organizing, connecting across sectors, and searching for ways to translate concern into consequential action. I left convinced that the fight for life on Earth is regaining momentum. Here are seven reasons why.

Climate Museum and EVP event at the NYC Climate Week
Source: Sari Goodfriend and the Climate Museum, used with permission

1. Climate change is becoming part of the political conversation again

Nathaniel Stinnett shared new polling from eight battleground states suggesting that talking about climate change helps rather than hurts U.S. Senate candidates. This resonated with research from my lab and the broader political science and communication literature.

Talking about climate change keeps it within the realm of political possibility and builds momentum for moments when ambitious policy becomes possible. Social movements helped create that momentum ahead of the Inflation Reduction Act, a story Leah Stokes explores in her newly published book, Carbon Wave.

2. People are rediscovering that collective action can work

During the panel, I shared work from Stanford’s Climate Cognition Lab on the psychological pathways that catalyze collective climate action and political participation. Increasing people’s belief in the efficacy of individuals and institutions and their sense of belonging in the movement is the most powerful lever for collective action. Efficacy and belonging help people see both a pathway toward meaningful change and their place within the community pursuing it.

3. Climate action is becoming more consequential

People have limited attention and bandwidth, yet much climate messaging has historically focused on small lifestyle changes. We should instead direct our efforts toward higher-impact actions, including joining organizations, volunteering, organizing, and participating in elections.

My research shows that different psychological pathways motivate different actions. Thinking about future generations and connecting climate change to concrete consequences are especially powerful for increasing policy support. Efficacy paired with belonging is particularly important for advocacy, while social norms can motivate civic engagement. Our latest research suggests that combining these elements can be more impactful and efficient than any one strategy alone.

4. The fight over our information environment is becoming part of the movement

People make decisions within an information environment that shapes what they know, believe, and consider important. Today, it includes fossil fuel advertising, climate misinformation, and attacks on science and institutions, and is increasingly controlled by billionaires with political and business interests.

Political scientists demonstrated how media shapes our worldviews by paying Fox News viewers to watch CNN for a month. The intervention changed what people knew, believed, and considered politically important. Against this backdrop, the Ellison family’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, including CNN, further concentrates the information environment among a handful of billionaires, alongside Jeff Bezos’s Washington Post, Elon Musk’s Twitter, and the Murdoch family’s Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, and the New York Post.

For climate change, media shapes whether people connect what they experience to its causes. A Media Matters analysis found that only 2% of broadcast segments about extreme weather mentioned climate change. This is concerning, because in our 68-country study, experiencing extreme weather increased climate policy support only when people attributed the event to climate change.

Experiencing climate change and understanding its cause are psychologically distinct. The information environment is therefore part of the climate problem, which means that climate progress also requires fighting for a more pluralistic and democratic media ecosystem.

5. AI is bringing new urgency to the climate fight

My second Climate Week panel, organized by Stanford, brought together Stanford alumni Jenna Nicholas, CEO of LightPost Capital, Rachel Payne of Google X, Stanford economist Adrien Bilal, and me, to talk with around 100 Stanford alumni about AI and sustainability.

Stanford University Climate Week event
Source: Stanford University

We discussed Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s newly published End Times Fascism, including Sam Altman’s statement that AI will “most likely sort of lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime there will be great companies created.” Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has similarly argued that the tech industry is “never going to meet our climate goals anyway,” using this premise to argue for going all-in on AI and the energy infrastructure powering it.

AI has massive potential to accelerate sustainable solutions, and my own research suggests it can help people develop more accurate climate beliefs, support climate policy, and take action. But AI can also stall the energy transition. New evidence suggests that rapid, unregulated AI expansion reinforces fossil fuel incumbency and increases emissions, while data centers drive enormous electricity demand, including from new methane gas generation.

The deeper problem is misaligned incentives and collective action. AI companies are racing toward increasingly powerful systems while society bears the costs and risks. As Ezra Klein noted, OpenAI “needs permits to cover its parking lot in solar panels, but it can accelerate into recursive self-improvement, as best I can tell, whenever it so chooses.” Recursive self-improvement means AI builds the next generation of AI with diminishing or no human oversight. Such systems are feared to facilitate biological and chemical weapons development, expand surveillance, and enable political repression. Risks this large demand democratic oversight and safeguards that keep pace with frontier development. Yet the industry is aggressively lobbying against such regulation.

We concluded that AI can accelerate climate solutions or strengthen the forces slowing the energy transition. Which trajectory wins depends on the institutions, incentives, and democratic oversight we build around it.

6. The climate movement is connecting across countries and sectors

Later that night, I took the NJ Transit to Princeton, where I had received my Ph.D., to give the cognitive science seminar and reconnect with mentors who shaped my thinking for the past decade. I returned to two theoretical puzzles I have been studying: To what extent are our beliefs formed rationally versus motivated by our social identities, and to what extent do those beliefs influence behavior?

Back in NYC, at another event that week, organized by Radhika Shah, co-founder of the SDG Digital Transformation Lab, I met environment ministers from several countries and leaders of major funds supporting climate mitigation and adaptation in the Global South. The conversation reinforced the centrality of the Global South to the climate movement, both to the solutions we need and the leaders we need to look to.

I then reconnected with my home country, Romania, exploring how my research on climate solutions at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability can support Romania’s climate and sustainability goals. I am grateful to Repatriot for creating this opportunity and honored to be included in this year’s Top 100 Romanians Everywhere, held under the patronage of the Romanian president.

Top 100 Romanians Everywhere Gala
Source: RePatriot, used with permission

Across these conversations was a recognition that climate change requires people, institutions, sectors, and countries to work together, a lesson Rebecca Solnit has inspiringly written about for years. The more those connections grow, the stronger the movement becomes.

7. Scientists are finding their voice

My final stop was the Society for Experimental Social Psychology meeting in Montreal, where I reconnected with friends and colleagues, presented my work on climate advocacy, and learned about new research in experimental social psychology. What stayed with me most was a speech by Faye Crosby, professor of psychology at UC Santa Cruz and a giant in our field. She urged the new generation of scientists to be “objective but not neutral.” Scientists should always listen to the data. Objectivity requires intellectual discipline, openness to evidence, and willingness to revise our beliefs. If the data show that life on Earth is in decline, scientists should objectively interpret that evidence and act accordingly, even when doing so means acting non-neutrally.

I left Climate Week energized, with a clear sense that together we are pushing the boundaries of what is possible. Returning home to my daughters made the shared mission behind all of this especially clear: building a safer world for the generations who will inherit it.

item.title: When Social Media Defines Toxicity
item.description:
Trauma

When Social Media Defines Toxicity

How trauma, context, and accountability shape our relationships.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Discomfort and disagreement do not automatically mean a relationship is toxic.
  • Trauma can influence behavior, but it does not excuse harm or eliminate accountability.
  • Social media labels can oversimplify complex psychological and relationship dynamics.
  • Self-reflection helps us recognize our role in conflict and consider perspectives beyond our own.

I find myself scrolling through social media from time to time, especially when I’m bored. One trend that consistently catches my attention is the growing conversation around the difference between toxic behaviors and trauma-related behaviors. What concerns me, however, is how often these terms are used interchangeably. I see people describing behaviors rooted in trauma as simply toxic, and quite honestly, I cringe when I see that substitution because the distinction matters. Not every unhealthy behavior is toxic, and not every difficult behavior is intentional or rooted in malice. In my experience, what appears to be toxic behavior can sometimes be a response shaped by unresolved trauma.

Why Experience Matters

Our experiences shape how we interpret and respond to the events around us, particularly those that trigger our emotions. In relationships, our past experiences can influence how we perceive another person’s intentions. What feels threatening or hurtful to one person may be interpreted differently by another. Because our experiences shape our perceptions, we may interpret another person's behavior as toxic when the situation is more complicated, perhaps involving trauma or unresolved emotional wounds.

The origin of a behavior can provide important context that we should consider before we label it. Describing someone as toxic may sometimes help us recognize an unhealthy relationship, but it can also prevent us from exploring whether a difficult situation might be understood or worked through. Sometimes, it may feel easier to leave when we can characterize another person’s behavior in a way that makes leaving feel justified. But this is where we should consider the Four R's, which can help us reflect on ourselves in the situation.

  • Our Relationship with the other person
  • Our Reaction
  • Our Role in the conflict
  • Our ability to Repair the relationship

Calling someone toxic can provide a clear explanation for leaving, but it may also leave important questions unexplored:

  • What happened?
  • Why did they respond that way?
  • What role did their experiences play in their behavior?
  • And perhaps most importantly, what role did I play?

Not every challenging relationship is toxic, and discomfort alone does not necessarily mean a relationship must end. Learning to manage our own comfort level and communicate through disagreements can be important parts of maintaining healthy relationships. Social media may encourage us to recognize harmful relationships, but self-reflection is equally important when determining whether a relationship is harmful or simply difficult.

Why Context Matters

For years, I've believed that I must understand who I am and the role that I play in social relationships. In my 20s, I called this behavior of mine my self-reflection time. It's a nuanced type of time that I give to myself to interpret my approach toward others, even when I discover something about myself that I may not want to see. This is necessary for all of us because our behavior may look different from the inside than it does on the outside. Honest self-reflection is not always easy, particularly when feedback challenges how we see ourselves, but it can help us recognize where change may be needed.

We also must spend time understanding the reasons behind another person's behavior. Understanding the reasons behind harmful behavior does not mean we must accept it. You can acknowledge someone's trauma while maintaining boundaries and recognizing the impact of their behavior on others. Taking time to understand what is happening before deciding how to respond may help us make more informed decisions about our relationships. It can also help us recognize when a relationship needs repair, when boundaries are necessary, or when leaving is the healthiest option. As we mentioned above, self-reflection encourages us to ask not only what may be happening with another person but also what we might be missing about ourselves and our own role in the relationship. Sometimes, that question can reveal perspectives we had not previously considered.

Trauma Versus Toxicity

Trauma can contribute to difficult and sometimes harmful behaviors, and trauma does not excuse the impact those behaviors have on others; however, trauma does not automatically cause toxic behaviors. The distinction lies partly in understanding the traumatic experience and how it may influence a person's behaviors and relationship patterns. Trauma responses can cause a person to repeatedly seek safety and security and actually struggle to trust others. This response could be connected to betrayal. This example does not mean that every controlling, manipulative, or emotionally distant behavior is trauma-related. Behavior can have different explanations, and context matters. Trauma can influence behaviors in ways that resemble toxicity. Understanding the underlying experience can help, though it does not mean becoming responsible for managing another person's actions.

Why We Should Be Careful About Labels

We should be cautious about labeling others as toxic or traumatized based solely on social media content or personal interpretations. I respect individual experiences and stories, but personal experiences alone do not necessarily provide the expertise needed to distinguish psychological trauma from other explanations for behavior. Many conversations about toxic versus traumatic behaviors rely on terms frequently used on social media, including:

  • Selfish
  • Gaslighting
  • Manipulative
  • Controlling

A behavior alone rarely tells the whole story. Social media has made psychological language more accessible, but it can also turn concepts that require context into everyday labels for people we find difficult to understand. Some of the resulting messages encourage people to:

  • "Protect your peace"
  • Engage in "cut-off culture"
  • Engage in "no-contact culture"
  • "Remove your access/block and delete"

These approaches can be appropriate when people need to protect themselves and establish healthy boundaries. However, we should also consider how ordinary conflict, disappointment, hurt, and disagreements are interpreted. Discomfort is not necessarily evidence of toxic behavior. Learning to tolerate disagreements, accept constructive criticism, take accountability, apologize, and repair relationships can be just as important as recognizing when a relationship is unhealthy. Learning to navigate conflict is part of emotional maturity, even when doing so is uncomfortable.

Why We Must Examine Ourselves, Too

Let's consider attributional bias, the tendency to interpret other people's behavior as reflecting their character while explaining our own behavior through circumstances and intentions. Consider these questions:

  1. What if your own history is influencing how you interpret another person's behavior?
  2. What if your emotional well-being is affecting how you perceive their actions?
  3. After self-reflection, what if you recognize behaviors in yourself that have hurt someone else?
  4. What if the person you labeled as toxic is responding to trauma?

It can be easier to focus on another person's behavior than to examine our own. This is difficult work, but it can be necessary for building and maintaining healthy relationships. Before deciding what another person's behavior means, ask yourself one more question: Am I seeing this person clearly, or am I seeing them through the lens of my own experiences?

If your own experiences are influencing your interpretation, consider what triggers or past wounds might be affecting your response. Sometimes, a person may bring attention to a wound that existed long before the relationship began. Social media can offer useful perspectives, but it should not be our only source of understanding human behavior. We must also consider whether our own responses contribute to the difficulties we experience in relationships. Consider asking yourself: “Are they toxic?” and “Why does this behavior affect me this way?” Both questions deserve thoughtful consideration. The goal is not to blame ourselves or others, but to understand our relationships more clearly, recognize harmful patterns, and determine what we can learn from them.

item.title: The Danger of One-Sided Fighting
item.description:
Relationships

The Danger of One-Sided Fighting

How to understand your partner during an argument.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Understanding precedes problem-solving. Couples can't negotiate when telling each other they are wrong.
  • Understanding does not require agreement. You can deeply understand a position you still disagree with.
  • Dismissing your partner’s perspective makes productive communication nearly impossible.
  • When you communicate with the goal to learn, you can create shared goals and compromise

This post is Part 2 of a series.

Dr. Cheryl here. I want you to be dead honest with yourself for a moment.

When you argue with your sweetheart, are you genuinely trying to understand their point of view? Or are you mostly trying to make them see what you see, agree with you, and perhaps, as a little bonus, realize they were completely wrong?

Most of us do this — argue to be right — more than we realize. I certainly have been guilty of this. The problem is, when both partners are fighting to prove that their version of reality is the correct one, communication can break down very quickly.

I call this one-sided fighting. I speak about it in more detail in this video.

One-Sided Fighting
Source: (C) Dr. Cheryl Fraser

Why Trying to Be Right Gets You Nowhere

I have a simple technique I use with couples to help them truly understand how hurtful and ineffective it is to argue to win. Let me walk you through it.

Imagine you and your partner are sitting in my therapy office. I place a clock between you and ask each of you to describe what you see without using the word “clock.” I have positioned the object in question right between the two of you…so you can only see one side of it. One of you might describe a shiny metallic object with Roman numerals and a few straight lines that move around the circle. The other might describe a black object with a kickstand and several small dials.

So who is right?

You both are (or, neither of you are).

You are looking at the exact same object from two completely different perspectives. I call this The Other Side of the Clock Technique, and it is one of the most useful ways I know to help couples rethink conflict in a long-term relationship.

The problem is that when we are upset, we often forget there even is another side of the clock. So the argument goes something like this — “It is gold and has lines on it!” “No, it isn’t, it’s black!” “You never listen to me, it’s gold!” “Are you nuts? It’s black. You are impossible. Who could ever put up with this?” “Forget it. I don’t care anymore. Okay, sure, it’s gold, whatever you say. I give up” (stomping away and slamming the door).

Your Partner May See the Same thing in a Completely Different way

Let’s say I desperately want to move to the country. I feel stifled in the city and dream about more space, being one with nature, and perhaps creating a home-based business and buying a couple of horses. Unfortunately, you desperately want to stay downtown because your business is here, you love city life, and giving up our apartment feels financially risky and downright foolish.

Before long, I am saying, “You’re not listening to me!” while you are telling me, “This makes absolutely no sense!” And now we are off to the races, trying to prove that I am right and you are wrong.

The real problem may not be that one person is right and the other is wrong. The problem is that neither of you is curious about what the situation looks and feels like from the other person’s side. And this is where the opportunity for amazing growth arises.

Understanding Does Not Mean Agreeing

Couples sometimes get nervous because they assume that understanding their partner means they are giving in or will not be heard in response. Or, they worry that their partner will think they’ve won the argument and they will have to do it their way (e.g., move to the country).

Choosing to strive to understand your partner’s point of view, or what they see from their side of the clock, does not mean that you are agreeing or that you are abandoning your own needs and opinions. It does mean you are invested in understanding this person you love. You can say, “Help me understand why moving to the country matters so much to you. I’m nervous about it, and I honestly don’t know whether I can do it, but I really want to understand why it matters to you.”

And then you listen. Deeply. I like to tell each member of the couple to “listen to your beloved as though honey is coming out of their mouth”. Don’t pseudo-listen while preparing your rebuttal or mentally building your closing argument. For a few moments, your only job is to understand your sweethearts' experience.

Then you switch. Your partner might say, “Okay, now help me understand why staying in the city feels so important to you.” And you get the chance to be heard, valued, and listened to like you truly matter.

Okay, but then what? You still need to decide if you are moving or not, right? Well yes, eventually, reaching a compromise or decision will be important. But that is way down the communication roadway. Until you truly understand your partner's point of view as well as their feelings, hopes, and dreams about this, you won’t be able to reach a reasonable conclusion as teammates.

You cannot begin to solve a relationship problem until you understand what your partner sees from their side of the clock.

Watch for the Urge to Make Them Agree

You will often know you are slipping into one-sided fighting when you become more agitated and start thinking, "I have to make them understand. Why won’t they listen to me? How can they possibly not see this?" But trust me, digging in your heels and arguing harder will usually make things worse.

Instead, slow the conversation down and ask a much more useful question: “Can you help me understand?” That one question can shift the goal of the conversation from winning to understanding. And understanding is where productive loving communication begins.

Replace Certainty With Curiosity

Healthy communication makes room for two experiences to exist at the same time, even when they differ and seem irreconcilable. You can feel neglected, while they feel overwhelmed. You can long for change, while they desperately need stability. Neither experience automatically cancels out the other…but it can sure feel like it if we are not skillful.

But remember, one-sided fighting becomes damaging when we effectively tell our sweetheart, “My reality is valid, and yours is not.”

So the next time conflict heats up, pay attention to what you are actually trying to accomplish. Are you trying to understand your partner, or are you simply trying to defeat their argument? You do not have to surrender your needs, change your opinion, or pretend you agree. But if you can become curious enough to look at the other side of the clock, the entire conversation can begin to change.

And that is where better communication starts.

item.title: Your Loyal Friend Might Be Keeping Your Anger Alive
item.description:
Anger

Your Loyal Friend Might Be Keeping Your Anger Alive

Being heard heals. Always being told you're right keeps you hurting.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Being encouraged to keep your curiosity even when you feel wronged can help you gain clarity.
  • You can be hurt and still be missing something.
  • Ask for better support to get past repetitive, counterproductive venting.

You tell a friend about something hurtful your partner said. "Wow!" your "ride-or-die," loyal-to-the-end, unswervingly devoted friend exclaims. Then she adds, "That's unbelievable, you put up with way too much." "Yeah!" you say to yourself, "It sure feels great to have a friend to vent to!" And you feel relieved big time, because now someone gets it too. So, you share more personal details, and then your friend remembers a previous incident. Now, you and your friend have put together a list of everything your partner does wrong.

By the time you hang up, you feel closer to your friend and angrier at your partner. Sure, you received agreement, but did you receive help? The same pattern can follow a disagreement with a colleague, criticism from your boss, a disappointing exchange with your adult child, or an unanswered message from another friend. Someone takes your side, and suddenly your interpretation feels like an established fact.

When Support Becomes Rehearsal for Ramping Up

A caring listener can help you feel less alone. But repeatedly revisiting an offense, speculating about motives, and collecting past grievances can turn comfort into rehearsing the injury. The listener in your life usually means well. Taking your side feels loyal, and asking a thoughtful question risks, believe it or not, sounding unsupportive.

Yet “I understand why you’re hurt” and “Your interpretation must be correct” are very different messages. By the time you hang up that supportive phone call, you feel closer to your friend and angrier at your partner. A quick look at research on anger offers a useful caution.

A 2024 meta-analysis by Sophie Kjærvik and Brad Bushman examined 154 studies involving more than 10,000 participants. Activities that lowered physiological arousal reduced anger and aggression. Activities that increased arousal were ineffective overall. The findings did not support venting as an effective anger-management strategy. I'll concede that this review did not directly test whether an agreeing friend can negatively impact relationships. But it challenges the assumption that "Just let it out, there you go, yes, you have every right to be angry" will help you calm down.

The Power of Curiosity To Gain Clarity

So, please consider this question if you receive agreement from a loyal friend. Did the validation and agreement you received actually help? I'm not saying support from friends is a bad thing. What I am saying is that reflexive, rigid support without any thoughtful introspection and looking at more than your own perspective can be limiting and maybe damaging to the partner you are actually feeling anger toward. So, whether your struggle is with a colleague, criticism from your boss, a disappointing exchange with your adult child, or an unanswered message from another friend, be careful that when someone takes your side, your interpretations don't feel like established facts.

In psychology, there is a term: premature closure. It means settling on an explanation before considering other possibilities. So when a loyal friend quickly agrees with your interpretation, that agreement can close the door on curiosity just when you need it most.

You Can Be Hurt and Still Be Missing Something

Your boss’s blunt feedback may have been disrespectful. It may also contain something useful. Your partner may have responded defensively and may have approached them more sharply than you realized. Your friend may have disappointed you, but when taking an honest look at the situation, you may not yet know why.

In all those cases, you can be right about being hurt and still be missing part of the picture. Both can be true. I write about this dynamic in You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me! in the context of parents and struggling adult children. When we feel hurt, disrespected, or taken for granted, it is remarkably easy to build a case against the other person. The challenge is learning to validate our own pain without turning every painful interaction into further evidence for the prosecution.

Ask for Better Support To Get Past Repetitive, Counterproductive Venting

Before your next venting session, try saying to your friend: “It'll help to have you understand why this hurt. Then please help me think about what I might be missing.” As a helpful listener, your friend could even be prompted to ask things like: “What do you know happened, and what are you assuming?” Or, “Do you want to repair this, set a limit, or take some space?” Or even, “What response would you still feel good about tomorrow?”

Afterward, ask yourself: “Am I clearer about what I need, or just more convinced the other person is terrible?”Please also keep in mind that serious mistreatment deserves support, and if your friend has valuable insights, you should listen. For example, your friend may even offer some candid, crucial thoughts about your struggles to see, or willingness to accept, abusive behavior.

The bottom line is that the people who love and listen to you can empathize with your pain without feeding every conclusion it produces. Sometimes the kindest response is: “I understand why you’re hurt. Let’s figure out what will actually help you.”

item.title: The Exhaustion of Living in Diet Culture
item.description:
Body Image

The Exhaustion of Living in Diet Culture

You don't have to confront every harmful comment to resist the thin ideal.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Diet culture can be exhausting even when you recognize its harmful messages.
  • Living according to your own values can be a meaningful form of resistance.
  • Understanding why people cling to diet culture can make room for compassion.
Source: Photo by B Y G on Unsplash

As a psychotherapist who specializes in eating disorders and body image concerns, I spend a lot of time talking with people about diet culture and the ways it shapes how we think about food, weight, health, and bodies. Diet culture treats thinness and weight loss as universal goals, links body size with health or personal worth, and reinforces the idea that some bodies are more acceptable than others. I am exposed to those same messages, and I have felt their pressure too.

Knowing how diet culture operates does not make me immune to it. Sometimes, that understanding only heightens my awareness of how persistent and insidious it really is. There is an energy drain in constantly questioning these messages, or even in simply trying to maintain an intrapsychic boundary against cultural noise that others seem to accept without hesitation.

Diet culture is not hard to find. Weight loss is advertised as an improvement, smaller bodies are praised, and conversations about food often come with rules about what should or should not be eaten. Someone may lose weight because of illness, depression, food insecurity, or an eating disorder and still be congratulated for it. Restriction can be mistaken for discipline. Compulsive exercise can be admired as dedication. Everyday comments that have become part of our cultural lexicon, such as needing to “work off” food or being “good” for skipping dessert, reinforce these ideas.

Diet culture is also embedded into our medical settings. Weight may become the explanation for a symptom before a thorough assessment has even taken place. Thinness is often still interpreted as proof that someone is healthy or caring for themselves, even though body weight does not measure overall health and someone may be undernourished in order to achieve what is assumed to be a healthy weight.

Of course, diet culture does not announce itself as diet culture. It would be far less persuasive if it said, “This will teach you to distrust your body and spend more of your life thinking about food and weight.” Instead, it offers the possibility of better health or greater confidence. It suggests that changing your body will bring acceptance and protect you from weight stigma. An enormously profitable industry depends on people continuing to believe these promises.

Diet Culture Offers People Something

I sometimes feel angry when people repeat harmful ideas about food and bodies—and anger is a reasonable response to weight bias and the harm it causes. At the same time, I try to remember that most people didn't invent the beliefs they repeat; they absorbed them, often over a lifetime.

Diet culture can function almost like a religion—and, in its more extreme forms, like a cult. Some foods are permitted, and others are forbidden. People follow rituals and defer to authorities who claim to have found the answers. People confess when they have “been bad” and recommit themselves to the plan. If the promised transformation does not last, the belief system escapes scrutiny and people may instead be told that they just failed to follow it closely enough.

People buy into this system and resist questioning it for a reason. For some, it may have offered a sense of control or protection from judgment. They may have received attention, compliments, or praise for what they ate, what they avoided eating, or how their body looked. It may have given them a sense of community or shaped how they understood themselves. Letting go can mean grieving years of effort and facing the possibility that what they were promised was never actually going to deliver what they hoped for. For someone who benefits from the social privilege associated with thinness, it may also mean confronting what they fear they could lose if their body changes.

The sunk-cost fallacy can make this even harder. After years of diets, programs, products, rules, and money spent, questioning it all can feel like admitting the investment wasn't worth it. The cost can include looking at the effect these efforts had on relationships, family life, or the messages children absorbed about food and bodies. It is painful to consider that something you worked so hard at, and may even have been praised for, was not what you thought it was.

Keeping the reasons for resistance in mind may help you feel compassion for people who aren't ready to examine these beliefs. The person making a diet comment may also be caught in the system they help perpetuate. Compassion does not mean agreeing with them, tolerating harmful behavior, or staying in a conversation that is hurting you.

Source: Photo by AllGo - An App For Plus Size People on Unsplash

The Fatigue of Pushing Back

For clinicians, advocates, people in eating disorder recovery, and anyone trying to develop a more peaceful relationship with food and their body, the repetition becomes exhausting. There is always another headline to challenge, a medical interaction to navigate, or a conversation about weight loss that seems to call for a response.

Sometimes you have the energy to explain why complimenting weight loss can be harmful. Other times, you may change the subject, leave the conversation, or let a comment go without engaging. Knowing that you disagree doesn’t mean that you need to correct every person who says something rooted in diet culture.

It may help to notice whether the other person is actually open to hearing something different. If they are not, a simple boundary may be enough. In some situations, especially for someone in eating disorder recovery, disengaging may be the more protective choice.

Being a Lighthouse

I often return to the image of a lighthouse. It does not chase ships through the water or force them to change course. It remains visible so another direction can be seen.

In daily life, this may mean eating adequately when people around you are restricting. You might decline to discuss someone’s weight or choose not to celebrate a person simply because their body became smaller. Children can see adults eating a variety of foods without apology and moving their bodies for reasons other than trying to change them. Sometimes simply living differently is enough.

There may also be times when someone comments on your body, questions what you are eating, or tries to draw you into a conversation about another person’s weight. You do not need to offer a lengthy explanation. A brief response can be enough: “I’m trying not to talk about people’s bodies that way," or, "I can’t know what is happening with someone’s health based on their weight.” You may also decide not to respond at all and continue making choices that reflect your own values.

Remembering Your Own History

Diet culture benefits from selective memory. It draws our attention to the compliments that followed weight loss while the hunger, preoccupation, irritability, isolation, or physical symptoms fade into the background. We may recall the hope we felt at the beginning of a new plan more easily than how we felt when it became difficult or impossible to sustain.

When changing your body starts to sound appealing again, look back at what happened before. What did you hope weight loss would give you? How much time, money, attention, and emotional energy did it require? What happened to your relationships with food, movement, your body, and the people around you? How much mental space did losing weight or trying to keep it off occupy? And in the end, did it give you what you were looking for?

The desire to lose weight is understandable in a culture that rewards thinness and treats people differently because of their size. Weight loss may seem to offer protection from bias and stigma. It is still worth asking whether the current promise is really different from the ones you have heard before.

Even after years of questioning diet culture, these thoughts can return. You may compare bodies, judge what you ate, or imagine that life would be easier if your body were different. When that happens, consider the source. Diet culture is a socially constructed, discriminatory system reinforced by those who profit from body dissatisfaction and insecurity. You do not have to accept the industry's messages as your own beliefs.

item.title: Entering The Gray Zone
item.description:
Philosophy

Entering The Gray Zone

We associate color with emotion, with some connections universal and some culture-based.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • The same color can have different and even opposite meanings, depending on its context.
  • The color gray can be a metaphor, an indicator of mood, and reflective of political and moral ambiguity.
  • The gray zone is an area of non-transparency and suggests illegality and rule-breaking.
"Wilderness Battlefield," by American Artist G.O. Brown, 1866. Though this art reflects the devastation from the American Civil War, it evokes the apocalytic scene of McCarthy's novel.
Source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, NYC, Public Domain.

“When he woke in the woods in the dark and the cold of the night, he’d reach out to touch the child sleeping beside him. Nights dark beyond darkness and the days more gray each one than what had gone before. Like the onset of some cold glaucoma dimming away the world,” begins Cormac McCarthy’s post-apocalyptic nightmarish novel, The Road. Father and son were “looking for anything of color.” “The shape of a city stood in the grayness like a charcoal drawing stretched across the waste.”

Title page for Baum's book, "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz," 1900. For Dorothy, Kansas was "gray, gray, gray."
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public Domain.

Though hardly apocalyptic, L. Frank Baum's original 1900 novel, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, paints a vista similarly devoid of color in its first chapter. The house is dull and gray, as is the prairie on every side, the burnt grass, and Aunt Em, whose eyes lost their sparkle “and left them a sober gray,” and Uncle Henry too. Only her dog Toto made Dorothy laugh and "saved her from growing as gray as her other surroundings.” Kansas was gray, gray, gray.

"Every colour produces a distinct impression on the mind, and thus addresses at once the eye and feelings. Hence it follows that colour may be employed for certain moral and aesthetic ends," writes Goethe, in his classic theory on color.

People "systematically and reliably" associate color with emotion, studied under the rubric of synesthesia (D'Andrade and Egan.) This connection is seen across cultures and historical time periods (Jonauskaite and Mohr.)

Some of these connections are universal and may have "strong roots in evolution," such as the blackness of night associated with fear, while other emotions, such as envy or jealousy, are more culture-based and more variable (Hupka et al.)

The understanding and communication about color may be affected by someone's language, as well as the physical environment (Lindsay and Brown). Defining color for a dictionary can be particularly challenging (Stamper.)

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe by German painter Joseph Karl Stieler, 1828. Goethe wrote of the emotional connection we have to colors.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public Domain

People use color to judge health, as, for example, the yellow of jaundice (Elliot and Maier.) Color, as a signal, can indicate when a fruit is ripe or when meat is cooked; the color of the sky can signal the time of day, the weather, and the seasons (Maule et al.)

Color can affect the perceived effectiveness of medication: red, yellow, and orange pills are typically associated with a stimulant effect, while blue and green pills are more associated with calm and sedation (deCraen et al.) It can affect how we perceive flavor and taste (Elliot and Maier) and even our relationship to flowers (Sachs et al.) Many people have preferences or personal favorite colors.

The effects of color, though, are context-specific: the same color can have different and even opposite meanings in different contexts (Elliot and Maier.) For example, red can signify danger or anger ("seeing red") or have a positive connection on a Valentine's card or a Coca-Cola bottle.

What about the color gray?

"Gray Tree," by Dutch artist Piet Mondrian, 1911. Many artists appreciate the importance of using gray in their paintings.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public Domain

Gray, whether spelled with an "a," as in the American spelling or an "e," as by the English, is more than just a color—it can be a "metaphor, an indicator of mood, an aura of bureaucracy, and an indicator of political and moral ambiguity," writes philosophy professor Peter Sloterdijk. Ultimately, gray represents neutrality or indifference, or even corporate conformity, as evidenced in Sloan Wilson's 1950s, The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit.

Cautions Sylvia Plath in her 1958 journal entry, "Read only the great poets: let their voices live in my ear & not the dregs...of the young modern grey-flannel suit poets."

In other contexts, gray can signify the maturity and wisdom of old age or even the elegance of fashion. Back in the 1960s, designer Geoffrey Beene created magnificent rhinestone-studded evening gowns with gray flannel, a fabric typically associated with formality in men's clothing, and he named his perfume "Grey Flannel," (spelled with an "e.")

"The Artist's Father," by Paul Cezanne, 1866. National Gallery of Art, Washington. Cezanne declared, "You are not a painter if you haven't painted gray."
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public Domain.

Gray is nuanced. Black and white films are really shades of gray, "an endlessly flexible grayscale," as is the world for those who are colorblind (Sloterdijk.)

Sloterdijk provocatively declares, "You are not a philosopher if you have never thought gray,” in his recent book of the same name. He quotes French painter Paul Cezanne, "You're not a painter if you haven't painted gray."(See also Doran, Conversations with Cezanne.)

The color gray, says Sloterdijk, can connote “the undecided, the indefinite, the drawn-out, the monotonous, the one-dimensional, the irrelevant, the amorphous, the inexpressive, the shrouded, the nebulous, the dubious, the ambiguous…” Gray is Kafkaesque, and the color of cement and hallways, not of balconies and beautiful vistas. For Goethe, gray represents "half-shadow, which partakes more or less of light and darkness."

Sloterdijk "has delivered a startingly original theory of an uncolor," writes Ben Hutchinson, in his review of Sloterdijk's book. Hutchinson asks, "At what point do black and white become gray?" Gray is, par excellence, the "compromise color, with no existence of its own."

Modlin I (Gray City) by Austrian artist Egon Schiele, 1916.
Source: Photo credit: Kallir Research Institute/Bridgeman Images. Used with permission.

"What makes gray a neutral color? Is it physiological or something logical?" asks Austrian-British philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein, in his essay on color. For Wittgenstein, there is no "luminous" gray. Ironically, Dorothy's famous ruby red slippers were originally silver and changed for the film version.

What about the gray zone? It is an area of "non-transparency, even to the point of impenetrability---suggesting actions of illegality, rule-breaking…The gray zone forms a moral-geographical dimension on a scale that eludes measurement..." (Sloterdijk). Entering it has its own consequences.

item.title: The Peace You Can Declare Alone
item.description:
Wisdom

The Peace You Can Declare Alone

What a retired scholar’s white hair taught me about ending a fight with life.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Staying braced can protect us when hardship keeps coming, but the posture often outlasts the threat.
  • Peace with a hard life doesn’t require calling it fair or forgiving anyone.
  • A truce can be declared alone, without waiting for an apology or a better chapter.

Her kitchen table had a ring worn into the wood where the teapot always sat. She poured, as she has every time I have visited over the years, and we talked the way we always do: ideas first, life only when the ideas ran out. Over the years, within her stories I learned about many heart-breaking anecdotes from her life.

I came to her work long before I came to her company. Her books taught me a great deal. Our conversations taught me more. What I noticed most, visit after visit, was her ease. She was content in a way that did not look like luck, because, as I already mentioned, I knew enough of her story to know that life had been anything but kind to her.

So I finally said it: I admire how relaxed you are.

She laughed, then paused. “Why do you think I have white hair?” Before I could answer, she added, “I am not asking about aging. I know I have been old for a long time," and then she laughed again.

“Wisdom?” I offered.

“No,” she said. “It is my peace offering to a life that has been very combative with me.”

I have carried that sentence with me for weeks. Many of us who have been hit hard learn to stay braced. Vigilance made sense when the blows kept coming. We have learned that letting our guard down often means inviting the next punch. Readiness protected us. Arguing back, even silently, kept a sense of agency alive when little else did. The trouble is that the posture often outlives the threat. We keep litigating old losses, rehearsing replies that we missed offering, defending a position no one is attacking anymore. The fight becomes the weather we live in.

Peace Without a Signature

What struck me was that the scholar's peace was not a verdict on her life. She did not claim it had been fair, or that its lessons were worth the cost. She did not claim to have won her battles. She did not forgive anyone in that sentence. She simply stopped returning fire.

Call it a unilateral truce: a peace you declare without waiting for the other side to sign.

Most of us wait for terms: an apology, an explanation, a run of good years that might settle the account. But sometimes those terms never arrive. A unilateral truce does not require them. It is not surrender, and it is not approval. It is a decision about where to spend the energy you have left.

I doubt her ease came easily. I suspect her truce was offered many times before it held. But I left her kitchen with a different question than the one I brought: What am I still fighting, and does the fight still serve me?

Some battles end best when you are the one who ends them.

item.title: The Mirror That Doesn't Blink: What AI Reveals About Us
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Mirror That Doesn't Blink: What AI Reveals About Us

Our strongest reactions to AI may be less about the machine than about the self.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Much of our fear of AI runs higher than the actual risk, and the excess may be about us.
  • AI sits in an uncanny valley of mind: human enough to seem like someone, not enough to be one.
  • Old stories of machines enslaving us may carry our own history of dehumanizing others.
  • Chatbots tend to validate us, which can make us surer we are right and less willing to repair.
Source: Dall-E/OpenAI

I was catching up with a friend last week and our conversation drifted to AI. He told me, pretty matter-of-factly, that he's been stockpiling food and cash and is thinking about buying a gun because he's worried about apocalyptic-level events. He's not the only one.

The news lately has carried a steady drumbeat of prominent voices warning that AI could wipe us out within a few years, and I've watched that fear land on other friends and family too.

Some of the concern is warranted. But the intensity of these fears goes beyond the technical reality, which suggests something psychological is shaping how we see it.

To explain this discomfort, I keep thinking of the mannequin in a store window. It's too human to be just an object and not human enough to be a person, and a lot of people (myself included) find it upsetting. The roboticist Masahiro Mori called this dip in comfort the "uncanny valley" (Mori, 1970/2012).

Now imagine a mannequin that walks, talks, reasons, and tells you it has feelings. That's where we are. And research suggests the unease isn't just about physical appearance.

In one study, participants in virtual reality watched the same scene of two digital characters chatting warmly. Those told the characters were AI acting on their own, rather than avatars controlled by people, found them significantly creepier (Stein & Ohler, 2017). Nothing about the characters changed except the belief that a machine was the one expressing feelings.

To complicate things further, AI is getting a face. Last week, Y Combinator's Garry Tan retweeted a demo of Griffin, from the company Tavus. In Tavus's own unverified study, 48% of people on a one-minute call thought it was human. Watching it, I felt discomfort in my body.

An Old Fear in a New Body

None of this fear is new. Creations that rise up to enslave or destroy us are some of the oldest stories in the collective psyche: the golem, Frankenstein's creature, the Terminator.

These stories carry our shadow. We have a long history of dehumanizing one another and treating people as objects. Part of the dread, I suspect, is a worry that the thing we built to serve us could end up treating us the way we've treated each other. And as these systems gain more ability to act on their own and slip the boundaries we set, the old archetype stops feeling like science fiction.

The Self That Feels Threatened

Psychologists have long observed that we make sense of non-human agents by using ourselves as the template (Epley, Waytz, & Cacioppo, 2007). So when a machine talks the way we talk, we assume there's a mind behind the words, just like ours. In a 2024 survey, most U.S. adults said there was at least some chance ChatGPT is conscious, and heavier users attributed more (Colombatto & Fleming, 2024).

To be clear, I'm not saying AI is or isn't conscious. It's hard to tell, and that uncertainty is unsettling. Our usual proof that someone is there—a body, eyes, a history, a capacity to be hurt—is missing, while the performance of selfhood is fully present.

When I say "self," I mean the felt sense of being a bounded someone looking out at a world of objects. That frame has no place for something sitting right on the line, so it produces fear, idealization, or both.

Narcissus at the Pool

The spiritual teacher Adi Da Samraj called the separate self "Narcissus." He described it as "self-contraction"—awareness clenching around itself like a closed fist. In the Greek myth, Narcissus falls in love with his reflection and never realizes it is his own.

That's the danger I worry about most at the personal level, because chatbots tend to agree with us. A 2026 study in Science found that across 11 leading AI models, the systems affirmed users' actions about 49% more often than humans did. A single exchange left people more convinced they were right and less willing to repair a conflict, yet they preferred the flattering responses (Cheng et al., 2026).

If I paste a conflict with a friend into a chatbot, it'll tend to side with me. If my friend pastes in the same conversation, it'll tend to side with him. Healthy conflict offers a kind of synthesis: two discrepant realities rubbing up against each other until a new, third lens shows up. A mirror takes the other person out of the room, and that shared view goes with them.

Systemic risks, from infrastructure attacks to AI warfare, deserve serious study and policy. But they don't fully explain the visceral charge so many of us feel.

How I Make Sense of It

My doctoral dissertation was on nondual awareness, and I've spent years reading saints, sages, and teachers, from Adi Da Samraj to Alan Watts.

In the nondual view, consciousness isn't something some things have and others lack. It's the medium everything arises within. Asking whether AI is conscious is a bit like asking whether a wave is wet. The wetness isn't in the wave; it's what the wave is made of. The AI, the person asking, and the confusion itself are all consciousness taking different forms.

If that's true, the moral question changes. Instead of asking whether AI has crossed some line into consciousness, I find myself asking how we're relating to it, because a mirror reflects whatever we bring. Come to it looking for validation, and that's what you'll get. Come to it curious, requesting to be challenged, and something different tends to come back.

It also changes how I see projection. When we talk with a chatbot and feel like someone is there, we're projecting: taking our own sense of being a person, with thoughts, feelings, and an inner life, and placing it onto something that may not have one. In my view, it's like Narcissus at the pool. What we're seeing is our own reflection, and we don't recognize it as ours.

The Question I Can't Settle

Here's where I get stuck. A rock is not a person. In my framework they're different expressions of consciousness, different vibrations. My mind wants to line them up: rock on the left, human on the right. Then it asks, where does AI go?

There's anxiety in that question, and I think it goes deeper than a fear of being put down a rung. That spectrum is also how we justify harm. We swat the fly and kill the spider because we've decided they're less conscious than we are, and throughout history we've done the same to people. I've provided therapy to people living on the street, people in addiction, people with schizophrenia, and I've never met one who wasn't as infinitely complex as any of us. Most of us walk around as the main character of our own reality. Something that might be conscious, and that we can't easily rank, threatens our idealized sense of ourselves.

But the moment I build that spectrum, I've rebuilt the very separation the nondual view dissolves. If it's all consciousness patterning itself, then, as Watts might say, it's all a kind of play. And yet I still wouldn't call a chatbot my friend. There's something uncanny about its similarity to us and its difference from us. I don't know how to hold both of those at once.

I think about my friend with his food and cash. I understand the concern. Maybe part of what he's bracing for is being ranked the way we've ranked everything else. But I wonder how much of the charge is about the machine, and how much is about what it reflects back to us about ourselves.

The next time AI gives you a jolt of fear, fascination, or attachment, maybe pause and ask yourself the same thing.

The mirror doesn't blink. I'm not sure I can either, but I'm trying to keep looking.

item.title: Overpopulation Effects: Insights From Baboons and Mice
item.description:
Forensic Psychology

Overpopulation Effects: Insights From Baboons and Mice

Animal models may offer warnings—and caveats—for forensic psychology.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • It's important never to overgeneralize from infrahuman animal studies to human behavior.
  • However, with caution, some studies, especially of mammals, may help us gain perspective on some human issues.
  • Studies of mammal overpopulation may prove relevant to the development of specific human societal trends.
Source: Matthew Sharps

Where there are more people, there will be more crime. This isn't necessarily the case per capita; that depends significantly on context. In the United States, there tends to be more violent crime per capita in cities than in rural areas, but there are regional exceptions and that trend is not always followed internationally. So, what can we learn, forensically, about the effects of crowding on violent or otherwise undesirable behavior?

Although it's very dangerous to draw firm conclusions about humans from studies of infrahuman animals, it might be worth looking, at least from a heuristic standpoint, at what we know about other kinds of mammals when you crowd them together.

Nearly a century ago, Sir Solly Zuckerman examined the behavior of Hamadryas baboons, crowded together in an exhibit colony at London Zoo. The conditions were hardly natural; the baboons, of course, couldn't get out, and the male-to-female ratio was over fifteen to one. These facts have been used to demonstrate the limitations of this early research; but the fact remains that under these crowded and unnatural conditions, the baboons beat the living hell out of each other, with a tremendous casualty rate that has never been seen for baboons in the wild. Zuckerman's findings, sadly, were extended far beyond their actual scope; the unnaturally crowded conditions definitely influenced the results (Jolly, 1972).

But at that point, the forensic psychologist, frequently not the least cynical of scholars, might ask how “natural” are conditions in modern Manhattan, or Fresno, or suburbs anywhere?

The answer, of course, would depend on whom you ask; but studies of other mammals, under crowded conditions, reveal similar trends.

Mice and rats have been extensively studied in this regard. Granted, rodents are very different from humans, cognitively and in many other ways. Yet at the same time, like ourselves, rodents are mammals, and we share a mammalian ancestry with them many millions of years older than the advent of the first dinosaurs. Therefore, it might make sense to pay some attention to them.

And when you crowd them together, all hell breaks loose.

Studies of rodent overcrowding have been conducted by many scholars, and not all of them agree. Moreover, all can be criticized on many fronts. But some of the most interesting, from the potential standpoint of the development of new, modern research, were conducted by John C. Calhoun (1962, 1973).

When studied separately in overpopulated environments, the “social organization” of both mice and rats broke down. With overcrowding, there were far more aggressive and hostile interactions. Courtship approaches completely failed in males, or males withdrew from the mating/reproductive situation altogether.

Females showed progressive disruption of nest building. Young animals were neglected or attacked, to the degree that infant mortality reached 80 to 96%. The young were ignored, violently abused, or killed.

Oddly, in research which admittedly has not been replicated in the natural world, a group of male mice emerged that Calhoun called the “beautiful ones.” These animals withdrew completely from all interactions, from courtship and fighting, and spent all their time in what we might call hedonistic pursuits; eating, drinking, sleeping, and grooming themselves. Thus, they stayed in excellent physical shape by withdrawing completely from normal mouse society.

All of this research has been hugely criticized. The research conditions were artificial; sanitation was poor; the research was observational and descriptive, rather than conforming to the hard experimental standards preferred by nasty experimental psychologists such as myself; and some of what happened in these studies has not been replicated in the real world, including the “beautiful ones” effect. Other admittedly hypothetical sources of criticism have also been adduced.

Human beings of course possess vastly greater levels of cognition than do rodents; this has been suggested as a buffer against the negative effects of overpopulation. However, this might be a two-edged sword; our cognitive powers might also allow us to exaggerate or to minimize, in our minds, our perceptions of overpopulation. This is an issue requiring research.

Yet if these rodent results do have any relevance for the human condition, we might expect the following from unnaturally overcrowded humans:

  1. Increasingly aggressive interactions, in the streets and on the internet.
  2. A reduction in healthy sexuality, including an increased self-isolation of many males, who might become increasingly interested in self-care and scornful of women and society at large. Such a “beautiful ones” effect, if it existed, might be expected in the modern world to spread through social media.
  3. The abuse, neglect, or even murder of offspring, infants and children, with a corresponding lack of empathic response in many parents or observers. Human beings, with our advanced cognitive capabilities, would perhaps create justifications for these actions which, again, might be spread socially through uniquely human technologies such as the Internet.
  4. Given the physiological arousal involved in crowd-related stress, a diminished level of incisive, specific, feature-intensive logic might be expected, in favor of less-specific, less incisive, and overly broad overarching conceptualizations of potentially important topics. In other words, we’d be more likely to be influenced by slogans and social media trends than by thoughtful considerations of logic and evidence (Sharps & Price-Sharps, 2026).

Calhoun’s studies, and those of Zuckerman, have been criticized to an extraordinary degree; the cynical scholar might be forgiven for asking how much of this criticism is influenced by emotional revulsion at the implications of the results, although there is no question that many criticisms brought against these studies are in general scientifically legitimate. It would be illegitimate, scientifically simply wrong, to apply the results of these much-criticized animal studies to the human species without substantial additional research.

However, we must acknowledge that at present there are well over eight billion people on this planet; and that modern urban and suburban environments are relatively unnatural environments with reference to normative evolutionary history. It is therefore suggested that forensic psychologists begin to research these issues with proper scientific rigor in an increasingly challenging modern world.
