item.title: Why “Love Yourself First” Is a Relationship Myth
item.description:
Relationships

Why “Love Yourself First” Is a Relationship Myth

Love is not a two-step sequence. It’s a feedback loop.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • The idea that you need to love yourself first before you love others is a myth.
  • Postponing intimacy until you achieve perfect self-love can trap you in an endless self-improvement project.
  • Love is a trilateral dance: learn to love yourself, love others, and receive love at the same time.
  • Lack of self-love is rarely the sole cause of relationship problems; don't overlook other underlying factors.

You’ve probably heard this advice proliferating on the Internet: You need to love yourself before you can love others. Another version of this phrase is that unless you learn to love yourself, you can’t love others well.

Let’s call this the two-step approach to love: self-love first, relationships later.

On the surface, this advice seems appealing. Assuming self-love refers to, or at least incorporates, self-esteem, there is indeed research suggesting that healthy self-esteem may benefit relationships. A longitudinal study synthesizing research from 48 samples found that self-esteem positively predicted better relationships.

Perhaps having high self-esteem empowers you to love others better. And by this logic, low self-esteem might contribute to excessive reassurance-seeking, fear of rejection, jealousy, unhealthy dependency, or difficulty accepting care.

So the implication of the two-step approach is that if you suffer from low self-esteem, you should focus on improving your self-worth and delay getting involved in relationships. Otherwise, you might hurt yourself or others in the process.

Or at least that’s what conventional wisdom would have you believe.

The Two-Step Approach to Love Is a Myth

In their book Fight Right, Julie and John Gottman, two of the world’s leading relationship experts, label the idea that you need to love yourself before you can love others a myth. They point out that nobody can love themselves perfectly. Most of us will struggle with at least some insecurity and self-doubt throughout our lives.

This raises an obvious question: When will we know we have enough self-love to begin loving others?

The Gottmans also flag a negative consequence of the two-step approach. If you struggle in a relationship, you might assume that it’s your fault—you simply haven’t mastered self-love. But the causes of relationship problems are often more complex than your lack of self-love.

The reverse can also be a problem. You might over-pathologize another person when a relationship ends, attributing the failure entirely to their lack of self-love. Again, it takes two to tango, and you might be overlooking other relational dynamics.

Here’s another consequence of the two-step approach: You might be putting too much stock in self-love as a panacea for relationship problems.

If only I learn to love myself more, I’ll have a great relationship with my partner! Well, not necessarily.

Keep in mind that there are many other factors that predict relationship satisfaction. Even people with healthy self-esteem struggle in their relationships.

Most importantly, I worry that the two-step approach encourages people to postpone intimacy by cloistering themselves in a psychological cocoon. Let me be clear: I do think it’s important to work on your relationship with yourself. But you don’t need to complete that work before forming meaningful relationships with others.

If the two-step approach is misguided, what’s the alternative?

Love Is a Trilateral Dance

A study of 14,741 individuals in the Netherlands found that self-esteem predicted subsequent relationship satisfaction, but the reverse was also true: People who were more satisfied with their relationships subsequently reported higher self-esteem. In fact, variability in how satisfied people felt with their social relationships had a stronger effect on their self-esteem than variability in self-esteem had on relationship satisfaction. In other words, the effects are bidirectional. Positive self-esteem can potentially improve your relationships, but relationships can also improve your self-esteem.

So what’s a better way to approach love?

Perhaps love is less like a sequence and more like a dance. You could call this the trilateral dance of love with three components: loving yourself, loving others, and receiving love from others. Rather than treating them as sequential stages, embrace all three simultaneously. Think of them as dance partners, tightly connected in a positive feedback loop. Take small steps toward all three at the same time and allow them to reinforce one another.

Learning to see yourself as worthy of love can strengthen your relationships. But engaging in relationships, discovering that you’re capable of expressing love, and experiencing other people loving you can also strengthen your self-esteem, which could then enhance your capacity to love.

Don’t make love a sequential two-step process. You’ll be breaking the natural rhythm of loving and receiving love that’s part of what it means to be human.

Putting It Into Practice

Here’re a few practical suggestions for practicing the trilateral dance of love.

1. Embrace self-acceptance. Thus far, we’ve been equating self-love with self-esteem. While there’s no scholarly consensus on what self-love means, a recent article argued that it includes self-acceptance—accepting your weaknesses and flaws. Perhaps you’ll always be a work in progress, and that’s OK. That doesn’t disqualify you from having healthy, loving relationships.

2. Avoid the reverse two-step approach. If “loving yourself before you can love others” is a myth, the alternative, “you can’t love yourself unless others love you,” is equally problematic. That’s still a two-step approach, just in reverse. Your self-worth shouldn’t be completely conditional on how much love you receive from others. The trilateral dance involves pursuing all three forms of love—loving yourself, loving others, and receiving love—not making one conditional on another.

3. Avoid self-improvement purgatory. If you’ve just experienced a painful romantic breakup, I’m not suggesting you jump headfirst into a new relationship. It’s wise to pause and focus on healing. Likewise, if you struggle with self-love, there’s value in learning to accept yourself and see yourself as a person of worth. Therapy can be helpful.

But don’t postpone intimacy indefinitely because you think you haven’t perfected self-love. And if your pursuit of self-love has turned into a kind of perpetual self-improvement purgatory—more healing, more self-analysis, more inner work, but less actual loving—you might be on the wrong track. It’s time to get out into the world and connect with other people.

4. Don’t neglect platonic friendships. Relationships aren’t just about romance; they also include family connections and friendships. Psychologist Marisa Franco argues that platonic friendships are a vital part of our social lives, but they don’t always emerge organically. You have to take the initiative to make new friends. Initiating and deepening platonic friendships can be an incredibly meaningful way to practice the trilateral dance of love.

5. Self-love is not a panacea. If you’re having a relationship problem, romantic or otherwise, research suggests that a lack of self-love is probably only one of many factors involved. Recognizing that allows you to look more closely at other underlying issues, such as communication patterns, differing expectations, major life transitions, unequal effort, or a lack of quality time.

To conclude, you don’t have to love yourself before you can love others. You can love others while still struggling with shame. You can be loved before you feel lovable.

Once you see love not as a two-step sequence but as a dance, you’ll be more empowered to pursue it, with all its accompanying frailties, risks, and joys.

That’s exciting and also scary, because there’re no guarantees that all your relationships will thrive. But being in relationships, whether with friends, family, or partners, is part of what it means to be human.

And that’s a life worth pursuing.

item.title: How to Tell When a Crush Becomes an Obsession
item.description:
Relationships

How to Tell When a Crush Becomes an Obsession

Separating love and limerence: when romantic focus becomes fixation.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Limerence is an intense, involuntary state of unreciprocated obsessive desire.
  • Risk factors for limerence include insecure attachment and adverse childhood experiences.
  • Limerence involves unrequited love, not reciprocal romantic interest.

Having prosecuted stalking cases for almost 30 years, I have seen many red flags indicating the pathological progression of unrequited love. Yet in reality, many cases of obsessive focus do not lead to criminal charges. With unreciprocated passion, the individual who gets burned may be the one carrying the torch. Research reveals the details of pathological focus and fantasy, discussing the difference between love and limerence.

Source: Image by Terri Sharp from Pixabay

The Longsuffering Longevity of Limerence

Chloe Evans et al. (2026) examined the large body of literature and investigation into limerence, in a piece entitled “Love, Longing and Obsession.”[i] They define limerence as “an intense, chronic, and involuntary state of unreciprocated obsessive relational longing” for a specific person. Recognizing that limerence exists on a continuum, they focus on the pathological progression of impairing limerence, which they define as a form of romantic obsession that is involuntary, intrusive, and chronic.

Regarding the progression, Evans et al. note that limerence starts during adolescence and frequently reoccurs throughout adulthood—consisting of approximately five episodes, each involving a prolonged (about two year) “obsessive fixation and preoccupation” with a particular person. Risk factors in the background of limerent individuals include insecure attachment, adverse childhood experiences, and obsessive-compulsive cognitive traits.

Evans et al. note that limerence appears to be founded upon trauma and relational insecurity, sustained through obsessive-compulsive traits, and influenced by negative moods, particularly loneliness and sadness. Limerence is linked with anxiety, depression, trauma, maladaptive daydreaming; Evans et al. found in one of their studies that limerent thoughts occupy about half of waking life.

As individuals consider whether they or someone they know may suffer from limerent thoughts, it is important to distinguish feelings of limerence from love.

Limerence Is Not Love

Limerence involves unrequited love, not reciprocal romantic interest. Evans et al. note that limerence is an involuntary cognitive-affective state consisting of an intrusive, obsessive, “all-consuming longing and love” for the object of one’s affection—who is typically unaware of their significance. And unlike the development of loving feelings or romantic crushes, Evans et al. note that limerence is involuntary, longer-lasting, and obsessive, involving a hope of reciprocation and idealized fantasies of the person of interest. Regarding duration, Evans et al. note that limerent episodes can last for years at a time, and limerent individuals can transfer their obsession onto different targets.

Unhealthy Attention as Addiction

Evans et al. note the similarity between the features of limerence and behavioral addiction, which include impairment, emotional volatility, and cognitive preoccupation. They note that this comparison also includes obsessive preoccupation, mood modification—where emotional highs and lows are linked with imagined reciprocation or perceived cues, symptoms of withdrawal where distress is caused by lack of contact, conflict with existing relationships, inability to stop thinking about the target, and even relapse, where an individual resumes obsessive cognitions or switches feelings to a new target.

Evans et al. also note that limerence is different from erotomania, defined as a delusional belief that an individual who has status and social power is in love with oneself. With limerent individuals, there is no actual reciprocation, only the illusion of reciprocity through imagination and fantasy, which fuels the experience.

Detecting Red Flags in Pursuit of Relational Resilience

Fortunately, there are ways to identify risk factors that indicate a crush is evolving from focus into fixation. Maladaptive, intrusive thoughts about a stranger, acquaintance, or even a public figure are causes for concern.

Recognizing signs of limerence within oneself or others can prompt the desire to seek help for what may develop into an unhealthy addiction with maladaptive consequences upon current relationships and other life circumstances. Health and wellness prioritize both physical and emotional well-being, which are enhanced by early recognition of harmful thoughts and beliefs, in order to reduce anxiety and promote positive changes. And for anyone already struggling with unrequited obsession, professional help is available.

item.title: Choosing to Live After Losing a Child
item.description:
Grief

Choosing to Live After Losing a Child

Personal Perspective: Questioning whether life is worth living after losing a child.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • The pain of losing a child can make many parents question the value of continuing to live.
  • Such thoughts are best viewed as a barometer of the depth of our pain rather than suicidal ideation.
  • Dark thoughts of this nature often accompany grief spikes, particularly around anniversaries.
  • Such pain is ephemeral and can lead to hidden, existential gifts.

I am writing this post primarily from the standpoint of a father who has lost a son. I am also a psychologist, and some of that perspective will undoubtedly seep into my writing. I want to talk about how the grief that I experience over my son’s death is so profound that I often question the value of continuing to live.

I am writing about this topic for two reasons. First, in consulting with grief experts, I have learned that such feelings are common with parents who have lost a child as well as many people who have suffered a loss of a similar magnitude. It is futile to predict how a loss will affect grief in each person; however, losing a child is clearly the source of the most profound emotional suffering of this nature. My hope is that discussing the uncomfortable subject of losing one’s desire to live will resonate with some parents and provide a sense of hope for coping with their darkest moments. With respect to the latter, I will finish this writing with two approaches to coping with grief when it reaches its most excruciating levels.

I lost Bill four years ago. The pain of realizing that he is no longer alive pops into my consciousness, unannounced, at random moments. When this happens, my internal experience is that I have just lost my son, or that I have lost him only yesterday. I have this type of grief spike when I am asleep and dreaming, when I awaken from a nap, or when I encounter an experience that reminds me of who he was (e.g., seeing a drum line marching, or finding a long-lost picture). When this happens, I often flash back to the memory of getting a phone call from his boss that he had not shown up for work. These grief spikes are particularly frequent the month before the anniversary of Billy’s death. When they happen, I often have the internal message that “I would rather die than have to keep experiencing this.” These experiences bring up the question of whether my life is worth living. I am fully aware that I will have these thoughts about my son's loss for the rest of my life, and likely on my deathbed. So why keep on living?

It is critical that I make the distinction between experiencing pain at a level that makes one weigh the value of continuing life vs. considering suicide. There is a profound difference between the two. This article is not directed to people who are considering suicide when in the throes of grief; however, it would be irresponsible for me not to discuss the distinction. The risk of suicide, and thoughts of this nature, does increase in parents who have lost a child, particularly when their child is lost to suicide. Suicidal thoughts must be taken seriously and require a different level of attention and treatment than what I am discussing here. When people have thoughts of ending their lives and have a plan to do so, this warrants immediate professional care.

Before discussing coping techniques that are useful for parents in the worst type of grief spikes, I would like to mention that I do not believe that Stoicism is useful for this level of emotional pain. Stoicism has become increasingly popular and can be a very effective way of coping with many of life’s challenges. However, the intense episodes of grief that I am referring to do not lend themselves to any attempts to shut down emotion. In fact, I will be talking about the opposite, which involves staying with the emotion, as difficult as that can be. I also might point out that a common recommendation of the Stoics for losing a child is to never become too attached to one. I hope that I don't adopt such a wooden approach to emotions, because with the capacity to experience intense pain comes the ability to love more deeply.

How can it be helpful to go to the depths of our despair to the degree that we question staying alive? First, I want to make the point that we can seldom stop such spikes of grief; we can only remain on the train that is heading into a dark tunnel. Staying with our grief, rather than fighting it, goes against many instincts of human nature. But I have learned at least two approaches to staying with despair in my work managing chronic pain as well as losing my son.

The first is to grasp that when you sink into your deepest despair, you realize that your emotional experience is transient. You may think that your pain will never go away in your darkest moments, but in reality, humans are not able to sustain a feeling or thought in its current form for prolonged periods of time. Our neurophysiology is structured such that we are only able to hold on to a particular form of consciousness for a moment. In Zen Buddhism, there is the concept of impermanence; nothing lasts in existing form, including the searing pain from the loss of a loved one. When we experience emotional pain at this level, it may come with the thought that it will never remit or go away. People can reassure themselves that the intensity of their feelings will not last, and reminding themselves of this reality can help them cope.

The other advantage of embracing the searing pain rather than trying to escape it is that there can be hidden gifts that await those who embrace adversity. One of the hardest parts of experiencing my son’s death was grasping my own mortality. It is a strange experience to express that I wish I had died instead of my son, but that has brought some paradoxical gifts. I now understand life and death in a way that I would never have grasped without losing Billy. Stoics choose not to love a child too deeply; I choose to experience the attachment to life that comes with embracing the loss of my son. I have deepened my relationship with my living children beyond what I could have imagined. I have learned to value deeply the friends who bring prosperity to my life and learned not to invest in those who do not. I am now more alive and present with most of the personal interactions I have in life. With every deep dive that I take about the loss of my son comes a brief glimmer that makes me want to stay alive.

I will end on a personal note. Many parents who have lost a child face a similar struggle with questioning whether life is worth living. We each must find our own way, and there is no simple answer. For me, I have come to understand that my son died because he felt that he had to take care of everyone around him, including me. He struggled with sleep because of the pressure from both this and his work demands, and he took a counterfeit pain pill to help with this. As I have struggled with the question of whether I want to continue living after his death, I have come to realize that there are some people who depend on me and hope that I will stick around. I owe it to Billy to do so because this is what he would have wanted.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Is More Data the Key to Better Behavioral Health Care?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Is More Data the Key to Better Behavioral Health Care?

Promising tools and ideas are emerging in behavioral health.

Posted October 5, 2026

I recently returned from the Behavioral Health Tech (BHT) conference in Nashville, where clinicians, health systems, payers, technology companies, and behavioral health leaders gathered to discuss the field's future. Over more than three decades in psychiatric practice, I’ve seen a lot of innovations in behavioral health technology. A few have fundamentally changed how I practice, but many have simply generated excitement without affecting patient care.

This year, the tone was different. People still wanted to talk about what’s new, but the conversation had shifted more to how we use new technology in ways that actually improve behavioral health care.

Whether AI, remote monitoring, or biomarkers, it’s clear the future of behavioral health technology is in the data. We have access to more data than ever before. We can measure symptoms over time, collect information from wearables and other biomarkers, monitor what happens between appointments, and use AI to identify patterns across increasingly large datasets.

But more information does not automatically translate into better care. We need to decipher what information is useful and worth gathering. Below are four key points I took away.

1. AI and the Guardrails It Still Needs

AI has very quickly become part of nearly every aspect of healthcare, and behavioral health is no exception. Though I expected its application to be a hot topic, I was pleasantly surprised to find just as many centered on where its use makes the most sense and what safeguards should be in place.

That caution makes sense in our fields. Psychiatric diagnosis is highly nuanced. There’s considerable overlap in symptom profiles across conditions, and presentation can be affected by factors like trauma, comorbidities, medication use, substance abuse, and more.

AI is an invaluable tool for organizing information, identifying patterns, reducing administrative burden, and recognizing things that might otherwise be missed. At the same time, technology that can identify patterns is no replacement for a clinician who understands their patient.

Perhaps the most promising role for AI in behavioral health is providing clinicians with better, more organized information and guiding them to use it more consistently. Clinical judgment and responsibility remain with the clinician. As these tools become more sophisticated, clinicians and patients alike deserve transparency about what they are doing, an understanding of their limitations, and appropriate human oversight.

2. Psychiatry Doesn’t Have a Blood Test–Yet

Pshychiatry has always relied on patient report and clinician observation. We can’t send a sample to the lab and diagnose PTSD or ADHD. As we’re learning, however, that doesn’t mean biological tests are irrelevant to behavioral health. In fact, neurology is already offering a preview of their utility.

Blood sampling, neuroimaging, and wearable digital devices are already part of neurological care and provide valuable insights that shape treatment decisions, including clinical trial inclusion. As more biological, physiological, digital, and behavioral data become available, the challenge will be figuring out which information is actually clinically meaningful. Biomarkers can be scientifically interesting without necessarily being useful in day-to-day patient care. It’s key to understand whether a particular measure improves diagnostic confidence, helps us identify risk, predicts treatment response, or allows us to recognize improvement or deterioration earlier.

3. Measure What’s Worth Measuring

Behavioral health professionals have been discussing measurement-based care for years, and for good reason. We should be measuring how and whether our patients are improving. But routine measurement can also easily become another box to check. Adminstering the PHQ-9 at every visit isn’t valuable measurement-based care. What matters even more is what we learn from standardized measurements, and what we do next.

One session I keep thinking about asked what “better” actually means. Some view improvement as a drop of a few points on the PHQ-9. But what about other measurements of improvement, like how many patients reach remission, or how many stay in treatment long enough to benefit?

Single measurements provided narrow views into inherently complex lives. A PHQ-9 score provides important information about depressive symptoms, but doesn’t always correlate with how well a patient is doing overall. Patients with relatively low depression scores can still be struggling substantially with anxiety.

That doesn’t mean we should hand out more questionnaires, though. If we ask patients to complete scales constantly without a clear reason, we risk creating assessment fatigue without adding much clinical value.

I expect and hope the next evolution of measurement-based care will be less about whether we collected a particular scale and more about whether we collected the right information and whether that information informed care.

4. What Happens Between Visits Matters

The continued evolution of remote patient monitoring (RPM) and remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM) came up a lot at BHT, particularly as reimbursement opportunities in this area continue to develop. Behavioral health reimbursement has always revolved around encounters: a patient sees a clinician, and the clinician bills for that visit. But as anyone who has practiced for a while knows, this visit is just a small part of our patient’s life. So much happens during the days or weeks when we aren't seeing our patients, and we often don’t hear about it until the next appointment.

Remote monitoring bridges that gap and can include symptom monitoring, treatment engagement, completion of therapeutic activities, and other information that helps us identify improvement–or the need for further intervention. Reimbursement makes it financially possible for practices to support patients more between visits. Yet reimbursement shouldn't drive the introduction of a new tool or workflow.

I think there’s real potential here, especially if remote monitoring helps clinicians recognize meaningful changes sooner and support patients without another traditional appointment. If monitoring doesn’t provide meaningful clinical information or patients don’t use it, we’ve only created more work.

Putting It All Together

If one theme connected many of the conversations at the conference, it was how we make all of this new information useful in clinical care.

What matters is whether that information helps a clinician understand a patient more completely and make a better decision about what to do next. It also needs to be presented in a way that doesn't simply create more work for clinicians who are already overwhelmed by documentation, alerts, and data.

This is where behavioral health technology is beginning to mature: that was probably my biggest takeaway from Nashville. Incredibly promising tools and ideas are emerging in behavioral health. Next, we must learn how to use them in ways that genuinely help clinicians understand their patients and provide better care.

item.title: When Children Leaving Home Is So Painful
item.description:
Grief

When Children Leaving Home Is So Painful

With the closing of a chapter come new challenges.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • For some parents, the launching of their children brings a profound sense of loss.
  • Underlying drivers may include loss of identity, past losses, and withering of the couple's relationship.
  • Accepting your feelings, repairing the marital relationship, and recognizing past losses can help.
Source: Anrita1705/pixabay

When my son left for college, I have to admit I let out a small sigh of relief. Despite the lingering, normal daddy worries, he was 18, legally on his own, and in a place where other adults could look out for him. And, a pat on my back, he made it through those potentially precarious teen years without any major scrapes!

While many parents I’ve met over the years have a similar reaction to their kids leaving home, some struggle emotionally with deep grief and a profound sense of loss that can persist for months or even years. What triggers these strong reactions? Here are four common causes:

1. They simply enjoyed their kids

They were funny, always brought energy to a room, or were sensitive in a way that was always touching. But now that humor, energy, or sensitivity is missing, a hole has formed in the family fabric.

2. Being a parent was central to their identities

Just as some people pour themselves into their careers and define their sense of self by their job title, some parents do the same with their kids. And just as many career-centered folks struggle after retirement, these parents feel much the same—a sense of loss. Yes, they are still parents, but their primary focus and tasks have shifted as their children have become more independent and are starting to seek support elsewhere.

3. Over the years, the couple has put their relationship on the back burner

The fact that couples in the US tend to divorce after eight years supports the idea that the 7-year itch stage of a relationship poses significant challenges. The couple’s individual needs have changed, their lifestyle and routines no longer fit, arguments have increased, and many divorce. But rather than tackling these challenges head-on, some couples don’t. Instead, they sweep their problems under the rug and focus on their children, shifting from lovers to mom and dad.

But as the children leave home, that parenting glue evaporates, and the couple begins to realize how disconnected they have become, fueling their anxiety and grief.

4. They have unresolved grief about past losses

Like knots on a rope, losses are connected. If one or both of the parents have losses in their past that they never fully grieved—whether it's the loss of a parent, a past divorce, even a cherished pet—it compounds the grief they feel over their children.

If you are struggling with any of these issues, here are some suggestions to help you move forward:

Realize that your grief is normal

As the information above suggests, there are good reasons to feel a sense of loss. Acknowledging and accepting those feelings are vital to moving through them. The person who tries to push these feelings away through distraction or compartmentalization is setting themselves up for anger and depression further down the line.

Put your relationship back on the front burner

If your relationship as a couple has withered, you face two challenges: addressing the problems you may have swept under the rug years ago to better fit your current needs, and creating new shared interests to replace your focus on parenting.

Consider professional support

If you’re feeling overwhelmed or if your everyday life is being undermined, and if old losses are rising to the surface, consider seeking professional support through a therapist and/or medication. Even a brief stint of therapy can help you get back on your feet.

Be patient and explore

Recognize that you’re going through a normal transition as this chapter in your life closes. Like any other transition, you’ll get your bearings as you move forward, but you need to take active steps by thinking outside the box and exploring.

Welcome to your new chapter.
